stops.segment: The Sorbonne, Baltimore, and the Year of Three Books
stops.stop: Paris, Cogito et histoire de la folie
stops.date_confidence: [A] the lecture at the College philosophique on 4 March 1963 is attested (Wikipedia; Wikipedia, 'Michel Foucault'; Derrida, 'Cogito and the History of Madness', in L'ecriture et la difference, 1967). The coordinate is the pool's for the College philosophique and is not verified against a street address. [A] Foucault's reply is datable to 1972 and comes in two pieces: 'Reponse a Derrida', first printed in the Japanese journal Paideia no. 11, 1 February 1972, and 'Mon corps, ce papier, ce feu', a longer reworking of the same argument that rereads the madness and dreaming passage of Descartes's First Meditation, carried in the 1972 Gallimard edition of Histoire de la folie a l'age classique. [A] Jean Khalfa states that the two men stopped communicating for ten years; Derrida dates the end of the silence to January 1982, which is what 'not reconciled until the 1980s' in the campa refers to. Contradiction left standing, not resolved: some accounts describe both texts as appendices to the 1972 edition, while the Cairn.info collation of that edition places only 'Mon corps, ce papier, ce feu' in the volume, as Appendix II beside 'La folie, l'absence d'oeuvre', with 'Reponse a Derrida' appearing in Paideia alone.

stops.segment: The Sorbonne, Baltimore, and the Year of Three Books
stops.stop: Paris, three books in one year
stops.date_confidence: all three books appeared in 1967, De la grammatologie from Editions de Minuit, La voix et le phenomene from PUF, L'ecriture et la difference from Editions du Seuil (Wikipedia); no month is given for any of them and the stop defaults to 01-01. Three publishers are involved and no single address serves, so the corpus's Paris coordinate is used. The Nambikwara reading is Derrida's engagement with Levi-Strauss and is cited here rather than staged as a stop, since Derrida never went to Mato Grosso. The quoted sentence is Derrida's own, from De la grammatologie; the Minuit 1967 page number (227) is carried from the research pool and has NOT been verified against the edition itself, while Spivak's rendering 'there is no outside-text' is verified at p. 158 of Of Grammatology (Johns Hopkins UP, 1976; corrected ed. 1997). The translation is disputed and is not resolved here: others render it 'there is nothing outside the text.' The campa's last sentence reads the quote forward onto large language models. That reach is not Derrida's: it is a forward application licensed by an author's grant recorded in EXCEPTIONS.md, dated 2026-08-17, under a scope of one or two sentences. Derrida died in 2004 and is not on record discussing anything of the kind.

stops.segment: The Quarrel Over Iterability
stops.stop: Paris, Marges de la philosophie and the word iter
stops.date_confidence: publication by Editions de Minuit in 1972 is attested; month and day default to 01, and the pin is the corpus's Paris coordinate. The etymology is Derrida's own and is hedged in his text: he writes that iter comes from itara, other in Sanskrit, as a suggestion in a parenthesis. The pool's afterlife lens hardens this into a derivation and overstates it. Latin iter is in fact from the root of ire, and no philologist accepts the Sanskrit link; the move is presented here as his proposal and not as philology.

stops.date_confidence: the doctorat d'Etat defense on 2 June 1980 at the Sorbonne is attested, the accompanying address published as 'Ponctuations: le temps d'une these'. The pool's geography lens puts Paul Ricoeur on the jury and is wrong: the jury was chaired by Maurice de Gandillac, with Pierre Aubenque, Jean-Toussaint Desanti as supervisor, Henry Joly, Gilbert Lascault and Emmanuel Levinas (aphelis.net, 'Jacques Derrida's doctoral defense'; Peeters). It was a defense sur travaux and Derrida submitted no thesis manuscript. Columbia's honorary doctorate, his first, also falls in 1980.

stops.segment: Prague, and the Institutions of the Eighties
stops.stop: Prague, the narcotics in the suitcase
stops.date_confidence: arrest at Prague on 30 December 1981, planted narcotics, roughly three days' detention and release on or about 2 January 1982 after French government pressure including an appeal from Francois Mitterrand are attested (Washington Post, 'Frenchman Freed in Prague', 2 January 1982; Christian Science Monitor, 8 January 1982). The pool's geography lens says he was imprisoned overnight and understates it. The chronology lens says Derrida and Jean-Pierre Vernant founded the Jan Hus Educational Foundation in 1981 and is wrong: it was founded at Oxford in 1980 after Jan Patocka's death, and in summer 1981 Vernant became president and Derrida vice-president of its French branch.

stops.segment: Prague, and the Institutions of the Eighties
stops.stop: Paris, the College international de philosophie
stops.date_confidence: the College international de philosophie was founded in 1983 by Derrida, Francois Chatelet, Jean-Pierre Faye and Dominique Lecourt, with Derrida as its first president (ciph.org; fr.wikipedia); the pool's geography lens lists Chatelet twice and is one founder short. Month and day default to 01. Derrida was elected directeur d'etudes at the EHESS in 1983 but took up the chair in 1984 and held it until 2003; the pool's geography lens dates the post to 1983 and is a year early.

His text from the colloquium is collected as 'Pour l'amour de Lacan'.

stops.segment: The Language That Was Never His
stops.stop: Baton Rouge, the one language that is not his
stops.date_confidence: the oral version was delivered 23-25 April 1992 at the colloquium 'Echoes from Elsewhere / Renvois d'ailleurs', organized by Patrick Mensah and David Wills and hosted by Edouard Glissant at Louisiana State University; the French book followed in 1996 and Mensah's English translation in 1998 (translator's note, Monolingualism of the Other, Stanford UP). The pool's geography lens dates the delivery to 1996 and is four years late. The French refrain quoted is consistently cited across secondary sources but was not verified against the primary edition in this pass.

stops.segment: The Language That Was Never His
stops.stop: Capri, faith and knowledge
stops.date_confidence: the Capri colloquium on religion, with Gianni Vattimo, Hans-Georg Gadamer and Eugenio Trias, took place in early 1994; Derrida's contribution was published as 'Foi et savoir' in the volume Religion, edited by Derrida and Vattimo (Polity, 1998). The pool dates it 28 February 1994; the exact day is not independently confirmed here.

stops.segment: The Language That Was Never His
stops.stop: Paris, the tribute in Liberation
stops.date_confidence: Derrida's tribute to Gilles Deleuze, 'Il me faudra errer tout seul', appeared in Liberation on 7 November 1995, three days after Deleuze's death on 4 November; the pool's geography lens dates it 6 November and is one day early. Collected in Chaque fois unique, la fin du monde (Galilee, 2003) and in The Work of Mourning, ed. Brault and Naas (Chicago, 2001). gilles_deleuze.journey.json carries the Liberation tributes on its own file.

stops.segment: Survival, and the Name on the Slab
stops.stop: Paris, death in an unnamed hospital
stops.date_confidence: death on 9 October 2004 of pancreatic cancer, aged 74, is attested (Wikipedia; New York Times obituary, 10 October 2004). The specific Paris hospital is not consistently named in any account consulted, so the citywide coordinate is used rather than an address. At his death he had agreed to take up the Hans-Georg Gadamer visiting professorship at the University of Heidelberg.

stops.segment: Survival, and the Name on the Slab
stops.stop: Ris-Orangis, the name on the slab
stops.date_confidence: burial at the Cimetiere de Ris-Orangis on 12 October 2004 in a small private ceremony, with his son Pierre reading a text Derrida had prepared, is attested (Wikipedia; Find a Grave memorial 9580205; grave photograph via s-hayashi.tumblr.com; New Statesman, 2021). The coordinate is contested: the pool's geography lens gives 48.6572/2.4275 for Ris-Orangis, the afterlife lens 48.6474/2.4114, and the pool's own correction puts the communal cemetery at approximately 48.660/2.408, up to 1.4 km from either. The corrected value is used and is not verified against a survey source. Two incompatible endings are reported for the graveside text, 'Always prefer life and never cease affirming survival' and the sentence quoted here; both are attributed to the same address and the contradiction is not resolved.
